# Running One Complete Study {#sec-running-the-loop}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"In theory, there is no difference between theory and practice. But, in practice, there is."*
>
> — widely circulated aphorism
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** The aphorism fits this study, which compares a model proposal against a fixed aspect-ratio heuristic in an architecture simulator. The model's explanation fails a declared distinguishing contrast. It is useful because the recorded results are less exciting than the initial hypothesis.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
One bounded AI-assisted study runs here end to end. It produces a tie, a failed
explanation, and a recommendation to retain the baseline that still awaits
author confirmation. The record does not name the accountable decision owner.
What do the results support, and what remains unresolved?
:::

The earlier chapters supplied the parts one at a time. A represented design
state came first, then method roles that propose and predict, an environment
that executes them, and feedback that must be interpreted before it supports a
decision. This chapter puts those parts through one complete study and reports
what came back. The recorded study numbers come from a model runtime and an
architecture simulator. The local architecture outcome is no change under the
declared rule, the two proposal arms tie, and the model's directional
prediction fails the test declared for it in advance. The architecture action
remains `awaiting_author_confirmation`, and the record does not name the
accountable owner. A discipline that publishes only its wins cannot show an
architect what a loss looks like, which is why this null result is worth
working through in detail.

The run guards against changing the comparison after seeing the result.
Simulators expose many configurable choices, and model outputs can
change with phrasing. A study can therefore make a candidate look stronger by
retuning simulator settings, weakening its baseline, or silently discarding
unsuccessful model prompts. These post-result choices are the same kind that
produced overoptimistic, irreproducible results across hundreds of
machine-learning studies [@KapoorNarayanan2023Leakage].

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The shifting baseline"}
**The trap.** A design team celebrated a 20% architectural speedup from a novel accelerator proposal, only to discover weeks later that the baseline software was accidentally compiled without standard optimization flags (`-O3`). When the baseline was properly optimized, the entire architectural gain vanished.

**The lesson.** Unfixed baselines create illusions of progress. If the baseline is allowed to shift or remain untuned during an architectural study, any measured "improvement" is meaningless. This scenario is a composite of a recurring pattern in architecture evaluations, not a single documented incident.
:::

In a real EDA environment, the penalty for guessing wrong can be large. Waiting hours for a physical routing failure consumes far more calendar time and limited tool licenses than waiting for a Python syntax error. A bounded study makes those costs and stopping conditions explicit.

Before any model or simulator output is known, the architect fixes the
workload, legal array shapes, simulator configuration, comparison budget,
rejection criteria, and decision boundary. Fixing these choices prevents
post-result goalpost moving. It enforces discipline without claiming the
choices were intrinsically optimal. The fixed aspect-ratio heuristic is the
comparison arm that the model-based generator must beat
(@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization). This record should also
have named the accountable owner for the pending action, but it did not.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Preregister the workload, legal candidates, score, decision margin, and evaluation budget before any candidate is measured, and validate every model proposal against that legal space before it reaches the simulator.
- Report the architecture outcome, the AI contribution, the mechanism explanation, and the stopping decision as four separate judgments, and record a tie as a tie rather than converting it into an improvement.
- Test a model's directional explanation against a matched contrast declared before any result is seen.
- Audit a completed study for the question its own design could not have answered, including a comparison too narrow to separate its arms and a rejection check that never fires.
- Package a run with its provenance, inputs, and raw results so another architect can replay it, and distinguish simulator replay, generator re-execution, and an independent architecture check.

:::

## The Bounded Array-Shape Study

The study below applies the book's method to one concrete architecture problem.
It uses a three-layer XR-like GEMM slice as an illustrative stand-in for a
localized spatial-tracking question within the Lighthouse prompt from
@sec-moonshot, which asks for a 3\ W, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for
an XR platform.

This is a separate executed array-shape study, not the prospective cache study
carried through the preceding chapters. It applies the same study,
representation, approach, environment, and feedback distinctions to retained
runnable artifacts.

The prospective cache study, `XR-L2-CAP-A`, stops at a ready-to-run plan. The
book does not have a retained cache implementation and measurement path that
could execute that plan, so it does not invent an outcome. Its recorded status
is *not run*, and its choice among the 2, 3, and 4\ MB candidates remains open.
That is an honest stop under the lifecycle in @sec-architecture-20-ontology,
not a recommendation. The array-shape study is used here because its inputs,
tool path, and raw results can be retained and inspected.

The intake begins with the bounded-study questions from
@sec-architecture-20-ontology. The study fixes one local decision, a 32 by 32
baseline, fifteen legal array shapes, a one-percent change margin, equal
simulator-call budgets for two proposal arms, and conditions that stop the run.
Only the two array dimensions may change. The rest of the accelerator, the
host system, implementation, and product commitment remain outside this study.

The represented state required by @sec-data-representations-world-models is
small enough to inspect directly. It contains the workload matrices, legal
dimension set, processing-element limit, fixed dataflow and simulator
configuration, mutable height and width fields, proposal history, and known
blind spots. The workload is synthetic, the score omits memory traffic, and no
energy or physical-design model is active. Those absences remain part of the
state rather than being filled by general model knowledge.

The approach decision instantiates
@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization with one model serving a
generation role and one fixed aspect-ratio heuristic serving as the comparison
arm. Neither arm predicts simulator outcomes or chooses an adaptive sequence
of evaluations. Both submit three nonbaseline shapes plus the shared baseline
under equal simulator-call budgets. The heuristic is intentionally simple, so
a tie can show only that the model failed to beat this comparator. It cannot
establish parity with a competent human architecture study or with the
strongest practical conventional search.

The tool path follows @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces by binding
each candidate to a retained model call, schema, SCALE-Sim configuration,
input and report hashes, and typed execution status. The record also exposes
what it failed to retain, including the rejected schema artifacts and an exact
prompt copy matching the recorded hash. The interpretation then follows
@sec-feedback-verification-trust. Candidate scores are compared under one
frozen simulator, and a separate matched contrast tests the model's directional
explanation. Replay can recheck the calculation but remains inside the same
workload, simulator, score, and assumptions.

This intake reveals the chapter's limits before the first result appears. The
run uses a different local target from the prospective cache study, one
recorded model call, a weak heuristic, a narrow analytical simulator, no
complete accounting of human effort, and no materially different architecture
check. It can show how the complete system behaves in one bounded run, but it
cannot establish the Lighthouse moonshot or the general value of AI-assisted
design.

To make the problem computationally tractable, the study narrows the top-level
system intent from the full SoC to this synthetic workload slice. The slice
does not claim to have been extracted from a real spatial-tracking
implementation. It provides a bounded way to map a system constraint into one
local architecture question.

Instead of evaluating every geometry, the generator proposes candidates that
must clear declared rejection checks before simulation. In a production study
those checks could include die area and wiring congestion. This run checks
schema validity, the legal dimension set, and a processing-element cap.

One recorded model call proposes three legal systolic-array datapath shapes for
a compact three-layer matrix-multiplication workload. A fixed
aspect-ratio heuristic proposes three shapes under the same four-call simulator
budget. SCALE-Sim 3.0.0 evaluates both arms[^fn-study-arm-c08] under one frozen
configuration [@RajEtAl2025ScaleSimV3], and a declared workload contrast then
tests the model's mechanism prediction. The study excludes model benchmarking,
full-chip XR evaluation, and tapeout. It asks whether a no-change architecture
outcome, an equal-call tie, and an unsupported mechanism explanation can be
reported without being recast as an AI success. SCALE-Sim computes cycle
counts, layer utilization, and modeled memory traffic from an analytical
dataflow model. It performs no timing closure or physical design, and this run
enabled no energy model.

[^fn-study-arm-c08]: **Arm**: In experimental design, one of the parallel groups in a controlled comparison, as in the treatment and control arms of a clinical trial. The model and the fixed heuristic are this study's two proposal arms.

The experiment reaches a reviewable result, although no nonbaseline shape
clears the declared decision margin. The model and fixed heuristic arms tie,
and the model's directional prediction fails its contrast. The technical
study stops with a recommendation to retain the 32 by 32 baseline for the five
unique evaluated shapes. That recommendation remains
`awaiting_author_confirmation` in the machine-readable record.

Array shape is a real architecture choice. Google's first TPU used a 256 by
256 weight-stationary[^fn-weight-stationary-c08] systolic array
[@JouppiEtAl2017TPU], while TPU v4 uses 128 by 128 matrix units
[@JouppiEtAl2023TPUv4]. The change across generations does not by itself
establish why either geometry was chosen, but it shows that one family did not
treat array shape as a universal constant. The 32 by 32 baseline here is a
fixed reference point rather than a claim of global optimality among all
fifteen legal shapes. Another reader can inspect the proposal and rerun the
recorded simulator computation without mistaking that replay for independent
validation of the workload, score, or simulator.

[^fn-weight-stationary-c08]: **Weight-stationary dataflow**: A mapping in which each processing element holds one weight in place while activations stream past it and partial sums accumulate across the array. Keeping the weights still removes their memory traffic from the inner loop, which is why the array's shape rather than its raw size decides how much of it stays busy on a given layer.

Most of this procedure is familiar architecture work where an architect
defines the comparison, validates tool inputs, evaluates candidates, tests an
explanation, and decides whether the evidence warrants a change. AI
participation adds a proposal and explanation whose scope, output, budget,
provenance, and authority must be controlled. This integration neither changes
what SCALE-Sim computed nor grants the model authority to decide what happens
next.

## Preregistering the Study {#sec-executed-scale-study}

To maintain that control, preregistration fixes the terms of the study before any candidate is measured. The decision question, the judgments the record must support, and the constraints and budgets that bound the run are all declared first, so no later result can quietly redefine what would have counted as success. The declarations that follow are short, but they are what makes the study's numbers reviewable rather than curated.

### Defining the Decision

The architecture question is deliberately narrow to test a precise hypothesis without overextending the methodology.

> Under the declared local rule, does any candidate selected by the recorded
> model or fixed aspect-ratio heuristic warrant follow-up over the 32 by 32
> baseline, and does the model's directional prediction survive its declared
> contrast?

A 32 by 32 matrix unit was selected before execution as a compact, square
reference, not on a claim of optimality. The architect also held a prior that
elongated shapes could cost wire length, an axis this simulator does not
measure. The fixed aspect-ratio rule is a simple and weak proposer. A tie
against it shows only that the model did not beat that rule under the equal
simulator-call budget. It says nothing about how either would compare with a
competent human architecture study.

The workload contains three synthetic GEMM[^fn-gemm-c08] layers used as an
XR-like stand-in. It is not a trace from a spatial-tracking pipeline or a
complete XR application. Their (M, N, K) dimensions are 128 by 128 by 256, 64
by 192 by 128, and 32 by 128 by 192. The mechanism test exchanges M and N in
the two nonsquare layers. Recording these dimensions lets a later reader
recompute the tie and inspect the aspect-ratio rule, though it cannot make the
slice representative.

Only the datapath's array dimensions vary. Dataflow, on-chip scratchpad
capacity, interface bandwidth, layout, simulator version, workload, deadline,
and scoring rule remain fixed. This narrowness isolates array shape within the
declared model, but the preregistration omitted a resolving-power check. After
proposal generation, the two arms differed by only one nonbaseline candidate
each. The completed comparison can report that weak discrimination; it cannot
claim that the tie was inevitable before the proposals were seen.

[^fn-gemm-c08]: **GEMM (general matrix multiply)**: The dense matrix-matrix multiplication kernel, conventionally described by the three dimensions M, N, and K, that accounts for most of the arithmetic in a neural-network layer. An accelerator array is ultimately judged by how well its height and width fit the M, N, and K of the layers it has to run, which is why those numbers, not the layer names, are what a shape study must record.

### The Four Judgments

A candidate ranking does not answer every question in an AI-assisted architecture study, so this experiment produces four distinct judgments from different parts of the record.

- **Architecture outcome.** Does any evaluated nonbaseline shape clear the local decision margin over 32 by 32?
- **AI contribution.** Does the recorded model arm find a better score than the fixed aspect-ratio heuristic under the same simulator-call budget?
- **Mechanism explanation.** Does the model's directional prediction survive its declared distinguishing contrast?[^fn-planned-contrast-c08]
- **Stopping decision.** Is another evaluation warranted under the predeclared rule and current project scope?

[^fn-planned-contrast-c08]: **Contrast**: In the design of experiments, a specific comparison between conditions planned before the data are seen. The M/N-transposed workload is this study's planned comparison for testing the model's directional explanation.

These judgments can disagree. A model might propose a competitive candidate without beating the heuristic. A useful candidate might arrive with a failed explanation, and a bounded study can stop even though most of the legal design space remains unevaluated. The executed comparison below reports all four outcomes without combining them into a single claim that the model or the complete discipline succeeded.

### Separating Outcomes From Claims

The preregistration keeps the architecture-outcome and AI-contribution claims
separate. This deliberate decoupling enforces one rule. The generator proposes
candidates, and a separate simulator computes the declared quantities under
its own bounded model. The model does not grade its own proposal, and the
simulator does not become ground truth merely because it is deterministic. A
schema-valid model response is therefore not an architecture result. The study
runs from a frozen plan through candidate selection, execution, interpretation,
and four separate judgments (@fig-bounded-study-workflow).

![**One record supports four different judgments.** The plan is frozen before candidate selection, execution, and interpretation. Only after those stages does the architect read the architecture outcome, study-local AI contribution, mechanism status, and stopping result separately.](images/ch8_design_loop_workflow){#fig-bounded-study-workflow width="100%" fig-alt="Workflow diagram of a bounded study. Four stages run left to right: freeze plan, select candidates, execute and record, and interpret the record. The last stage feeds four separate judgments: architecture outcome, AI contribution, mechanism status, and stopping."}

Read the upper row from the frozen plan through candidate selection and
recorded execution to interpretation. Only the interpreted record feeds the
four boxes below. Those branches keep the architecture outcome, study-local AI
contribution, mechanism status, and stopping decision from substituting for one
another. The final box stops this bounded study while leaving the architecture
action pending, so completing the workflow does not itself authorize a design
change.

- **Architecture-outcome claim.** At least one evaluated nonbaseline shape
selected by either arm improves the local decision score over the 32 by 32
baseline by at least 1 percent for the frozen workload and simulator
configuration. The outcome is no change if none of those evaluated shapes
clears that decision margin.

- **AI-contribution claim.** With four SCALE-Sim evaluations per arm, including
the same mandatory baseline, the recorded model arm finds a score at least 1
percent lower than the fixed aspect-ratio heuristic arm. A difference within 1
percent is a tie. A worse model result is adverse. Equal simulator calls do not
equalize model inference, human setup, prior knowledge encoded in the heuristic,
or total labor. One model call cannot establish a population-level result about
a model family, even if it wins.

These two outcome claims were fixed before proposal generation. The mechanism
hypothesis follows a different sequence. The architect fixed a mirrored-shape
test on the original and M/N-transposed workloads, then required the model to
supply its directional prediction before any simulation.

The local score is

$$
S = \frac{\text{total cycles}}
         {\text{average layer utilization}/100},
$$

with lower values preferred. This composite is not a true Area-Delay Product
(ADP). For $L$ layers with work $W_i$, cycles $C_i$, and the implemented
unweighted average of per-layer utilization, the approximation
$u_i \approx W_i/(\text{PE}\,C_i)$ gives

$$
S \approx
\frac{\text{PE}\,L\sum_i C_i}
     {\sum_i W_i/C_i}.
$$

Only for a single layer, or under uniform scaling across layers, does this
reduce to a squared dependence on cycles. The study therefore treats the score
as a predeclared local ordering rule, not as ADP, a universal accelerator
metric, or a physical measurement. The 1,024-processing-element legality cap,
not the score, forecloses oversized arrays. Reporting cycles and utilization
separately exposes the ingredients the score combines, though neither reveals
an omitted axis such as memory traffic.

The retained runner defines total cycles as the sum of the `Total Cycles`
column in SCALE-Sim's `COMPUTE_REPORT.csv`. It excludes the separate `Total
Cycles (incl. prefetch)` column. The frozen preregistration says only "total
cycles," so the executable runner, rather than the preregistration prose,
supplies this distinction. Including prefetch would change the baseline and 16
by 64 counts to 17,371 and 17,500. Their 0.742 percent difference would remain
inside the 1 percent tie margin, so none of the four judgments would change.

A fair comparison requires the evaluation budget, workload, simulator settings,
rejection criteria, and decision boundary to be frozen before either arm
produces results. The frozen rules keep the two proposal arms comparable and
make later changes visible (@tbl-executed-study-protocol).

| **Element** | **Frozen rule** |
| --- | --- |
| **Workloads** | One three-layer GEMM slice, plus a versioned copy with M and N exchanged for the mechanism test. |
| **Legal shapes** | Rows and columns each in {8, 16, 32, 64, 128}; product no greater than 1,024 processing elements. These rules admit fifteen shapes. The cap is a declared scope bound for this study, chosen to keep candidates in a range plausible for a 3\ W mobile subsystem, not a limit derived from the power budget by this simulator, which was run here with no power or area model enabled. |
| **Environment** | SCALE-Sim 3.0.0, GEMM interface, weight-stationary dataflow [@ChenEtAl2016Eyeriss], 128 KiB per SRAM, and 64 interface words per cycle. |
| **Baseline and rejection criteria** | Insert 32 by 32 into both arms; reject shapes above 1,024 processing elements or runs above 90,000 cycles. |
| **Proposal arms** | Three model proposals and three candidates from a fixed aggregate-aspect-ratio heuristic. |
| **Evaluation budget** | Four SCALE-Sim evaluations per arm, including the mandatory 32 by 32 baseline; no post-result replacement. |
| **Model repair** | At most one complete repair response after reported schema or legality errors; invalid proposals consume the initial call. |
| **Decision margin** | At least 1 percent on the lower-is-better local score; differences inside the margin are ties. |
| **Mechanism probe** | Four shared runs comparing 16 by 64 and 64 by 16 on the original and M/N-transposed workloads. |
| **Decision boundary** | The recorded result may motivate a clearly scoped follow-up experiment or stopping. It cannot authorize RTL, tapeout, or a system intent decision. |

: **The comparison was fixed before evaluation.** Both proposal arms use the same workload, SCALE-Sim configuration, rejection criteria, baseline, and four-evaluation budget. {#tbl-executed-study-protocol tbl-colwidths="[22,68]"}

The workload, legal shapes, environment, and rejection criteria fix the
architecture comparison. The proposal and evaluation budgets prevent either
arm from receiving extra candidates after results appear. Because this study
meters one analytical stage, the budget row can record a flat four simulator
calls per arm. The repair and decision rules fix how invalid model output and
small score differences will be treated. The mechanism contrast challenges the
generated explanation, while the final row leaves approval outside both the
model and simulator.

A production physical-design flow needs a different cost budget. Its stages
can vary by orders of magnitude in runtime, compute, and license use, so raw
call count represents their cost poorly. Such a flow might meter CPU-hours and
license-hours, then screen weak candidates with floorplan estimates before
paying for detailed routing.

Predeclaring these choices forces any change to the candidate, metric, or stopping rule out into the open, where it can be checked against the record instead of silently validating a flawed candidate.

Preregistration does not outlaw exploration. It separates exploratory work
from the confirmatory run whose results feed the study outcome
[@NosekEtAl2018Preregistration]. Any run used to choose a frozen study choice
must remain exploratory and cannot also count as confirmatory evidence. Those
choices include the workload, candidate space, prompt, baseline, simulator
configuration, score, threshold, budget, contrast, and rejection criteria. This
protocol did not record prompt-development iterations or author hours before
the freeze, so total human effort remains unknown. A future protocol should add
those fields before work begins rather than claim that this frozen record
contained them.

Nor does preregistration intrinsically justify the
three-layer workload, local score, 32 by 32 baseline, 1 percent decision margin,
90,000-cycle cutoff, SCALE-Sim abstraction, or four-call budget. Each remains
an architecture choice that would need a rationale and sensitivity analysis
before a broader decision relied on it.

The 1 percent margin is a local decision threshold over deterministic
SCALE-Sim outputs, not a statement that those outputs are within 1 percent of
silicon. Running both arms through the same frozen model removes configuration
drift and may cancel some shared error, but candidate-dependent modeling error
need not cancel. This study did not estimate that residual error. The margin
therefore resolves only the comparison as represented by this simulator,
workload, and score.

Every rule frozen in @tbl-executed-study-protocol exists because a comparison left unfixed can be adjusted after the result arrives, and nothing in the published record will show that it was. An entire research literature demonstrates the consequence at scale.

::: {.callout-war-story title="Civil-war prediction and the margin that was a leak"}
**The claim.** A series of political-science papers reported that complex machine-learning models, random forests and AdaBoost among them, substantially outperformed the decades-old logistic regression baseline at predicting the onset of civil war.

**The gap.** None of those results reproduced [@KapoorNarayanan2023Leakage]. Each depended on a leak between the data used to fit a model and the data used to score it, most often imputing missing values across the training and test sets together before splitting them. The published record could not separate a real margin from a procedural one, and peer review saw only the margin. Preregistration alone would not have caught this particular fault, since a leak sits inside the declared pipeline and would have been frozen along with it, which is why the survey's own remedy is documenting and auditing the pipeline. What preregistration does block is the retuning, reselection, and goalpost moving that a fixed comparison forecloses. Once the leaks were corrected, the complex models did not beat logistic regression in any of the cases. The same survey found leakage across 17 fields, affecting hundreds of papers.

**The lesson.** Fix the comparison before the result exists. A margin measured against a baseline that could still be retuned, contaminated, or reselected afterward is not a measured margin, and no amount of care in the modeling recovers it later. This study's protocol is worth its cost only because it was filled in before a single candidate ran.
:::

### The Mechanism Hypothesis

As established in @sec-data-representations-world-models, general knowledge is
insufficient without explicit project constraints. The representation for this
study is small, describing one accelerator under one set of fixed conditions
rather than the accelerator in general. The fifteen legal shapes, baseline,
mutable array dimensions, fixed simulator conditions, local score, and
workload matrices form the explicit design state. Formalizing these variables
keeps authority over the design boundaries with the architect. In this
instance, the candidate representation changes only the datapath's
`ArrayHeight` and `ArrayWidth`, while the weight-stationary dataflow
[@ChenEtAl2016Eyeriss], SRAM capacity, interface bandwidth, layout, workload,
and simulator version remain fixed.

That representation is useful only if a candidate change can be connected to a predicted consequence. The model proposed three shape changes and predicted that a wider 16 by 64 array would better match the workload's N dimensions than its mirrored 64 by 16 alternative. It further predicted that exchanging M and N in the workload would reverse the winner. A fluent rationale can misstate the cause of a proposal [@TurpinEtAl2023Unfaithful], so the study records this statement as a hypothesis to test rather than as evidence.

### Fixing Environment and Roles

The roles are fixed before execution. The model and fixed heuristic select
candidates, but neither produces the local score or approves an architecture
change. Validation scripts may reject malformed or illegal output without
deciding whether the workload or objective is appropriate. SCALE-Sim
calculates cycles, utilization, and modeled memory traffic. The retained runner
derives the local score and result status from those outputs. Neither
calculation establishes simulator fidelity. The architect interprets the four
judgments. The technical record retains the pending status, but it does not
identify a named accountable owner; author confirmation remains pending.

That omission cannot be repaired by silently assigning an owner after the
results are known. The historical record can support a technical
recommendation, but it cannot show who had authority to accept it when the
study ran. Any later assignment must be recorded as a post-study action with
the assignee, date, local authority, artifact received, and conditions for
reopening or escalation. Until that happens, the study can close technically
while the architecture action remains unowned and pending.

## Model Calls and Failures

With the roles and constraints fixed, the architect invokes the model. The
retained study record says the model received the architecture question, legal
dimension set, processing-element budget, workload matrix dimensions, fixed
environment assumptions, mandatory baseline, output schema, scoring
definition, and limits on what the result could support, but not the fixed
heuristic's candidates or
simulator results. The surviving prompt is consistent with that intended
context, but its hash does not match the frozen record, so the package cannot
independently verify the exact context supplied to the recorded call. The
retained response proposes a design mutation by naming three candidates,
predicting qualitative behavior, stating an anticipated failure mode, and
offering a directional mechanism with a testable failure condition. The
architect evaluates this output as a candidate, not a final decision.

### Handling Toolchain Errors

The first attempt to invoke the runtime never reached inference. The
response-format service rejected the request's JSON Schema before any tokens
were generated.[^fn-json-schema-c08] This was an invalid request caused by the
study setup, not a model result and not evidence about an architecture
candidate. The schema-only correction was recorded before inference.

[^fn-json-schema-c08]: **JSON Schema rejection (detail)**: The record states that two constant-string properties lacked explicit types, so no model output or usage was produced. The preregistration amendment preserves the old and new schema hashes but not the rejected schema body or service response, so the exact failure cannot be independently inspected from this package.

Fixing the schema was a recorded setup repair, not a concession to the model
or a change to the architecture comparison. A harness driving a real toolchain
would need to distinguish setup defects, transient service failures,
deterministic tool failures, and candidate violations from the available
records. Repeating an unchanged input can help diagnose a failure, but
repetition alone does not reveal its cause. A deterministic wrapper defect can
repeat without saying anything about the candidate, while a candidate can
trigger an intermittent resource failure. Only a failure linked to a named
candidate property should become negative architecture evidence. This run
recorded only the pre-inference schema rejection, which carried no
architectural information.

Correctly classifying the retained failures is only half the accounting. A run
that discards failed attempts before writing anything down leaves no way to
reconstruct the cost of reaching its reported result.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The illusion of zero-shot success"}
**The trap.** An AI model generates a highly optimized architecture design on the first try, and the write-up presents the result as zero-shot capability, a first-try success with no examples or iteration.

**The mechanism.** The write-up omits the dozens of prior manual iterations in which an architect tweaked the prompt, added constraints, and fixed syntax errors. This prompt shopping hides the true human-in-the-loop cost, framing a heavily curated result as autonomous intelligence. The case here is a composite of a pattern reviewers report across AI-for-design evaluations, not one specific publication.

**The lesson.** Bounded studies must record all inference attempts, repairs, and environment failures. The true cost of a candidate includes the discarded prompts and failed runs that led to it.
:::

### Capturing Call Provenance

The subsequent call returned a schema-valid response. Since semantic validation found three unique legal candidates, no repair call was made. The complete response is retained, not only the candidate coordinates or a prose summary. The runtime exposed only part of the provenance needed to identify the call. The available fields bound how far its identity can be reconstructed, and missing values remain unavailable rather than inferred (@tbl-model-provenance). A production EDA run would fill the execution-environment field far more heavily, pinning the PDK version, standard-cell library PVT corners,[^fn-pvt-corners-c08] binary patches, and Tcl setup scripts through Nix or containers to prevent environmental drift; this study carried none of that toolchain, so the field is recorded as empty rather than left to inference.

| **Provenance field** | **Recorded value** |
| --- | --- |
| **Provider and interface** | OpenAI through Codex CLI 0.144.4, noninteractive ephemeral execution, read-only empty workspace. |
| **Execution environment** | None beyond the runtime above; the study ran in a read-only empty workspace with no EDA toolchain, PDK, or standard-cell libraries in play. |
| **Requested and accepted model alias** | gpt-5.4; provider revision or digest was not exposed. |
| **Time** | 2026-07-14 18:21:51--18:22:24 UTC; 32.90 seconds wall time. |
| **Settings** | Medium reasoning effort; temperature, top-p, and seed were not exposed or available through the runtime. |
| **Usage** | 13,223 input tokens, including 1,920 cached; 1,446 output tokens, including 516 reasoning tokens. |
| **Cost** | Currency cost was not reported, so none is inferred. |
| **Interaction** | One valid proposal call, no repair call, and no observed tool calls. Schema, output, and provenance hashes are recorded. The retained prompt does not match its recorded hash. |
| **Privacy** | No credential, session identifier, or private configuration is stored. |

: **Provenance is only as good as the runtime exposes.** The record reports the values the runtime supplied and marks the rest as unavailable rather than inferring them. {#tbl-model-provenance tbl-colwidths="[27,63]"}

Read down from the provider, interface, and execution environment to the model
alias, time, and exposed settings, then to usage, cost, interaction history,
and privacy. The decisive pattern is the boundary around what the runtime did
not expose. Provider revision, sampling settings, seed, and currency cost are
not reconstructed from the retained response. The table identifies the
recorded call as far as the available fields allow, but it cannot make the
hosted generator exactly reproducible.

Temperature and top-p control how broadly a language model samples among
plausible next tokens. A seed aids repeatability only when the provider, exact
model revision, and sampling implementation are also fixed. Provider-reported
input, output, cached, and reasoning tokens are accounting fields for that
runtime, not comparable units of engineering work across different models.

[^fn-pvt-corners-c08]: **PVT corners**: The process, voltage, and temperature extremes that a standard-cell library is characterized at, such as a slow-process, low-voltage, high-temperature combination. Cell delay and leakage change substantially from one corner to the next, so a timing or power number carries no meaning unless the corner it was measured at travels with it.

The retained files record a five-event chronology. The preregistration was
frozen at 18:19:48 UTC. The response schema was rejected at 18:21:00 and amended
at 18:21:41. The valid model call ran from 18:21:51 to 18:22:24. The twelve
evaluations were recorded during one aggregate study-runner execution window
from 18:31:23 to 18:31:42. That window includes runner setup and result
serialization, not only simulator time. These internal timestamps record the
claimed order, but no external timestamp or commit binding independently proves
that order. The execution record also supplies only the aggregate window, not a
timestamp for each evaluation.

Three limits matter when interpreting this record. First, the valid proposal
used one call and no repair, so later candidate replacement cannot explain the
outcome. One call cannot establish the reliability or expected utility of a
model family. That program-level evaluation requires repeated model calls,
strong checks, and a design space capable of separating the compared methods;
@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect takes up that problem. Second, the requested
alias is not a pinned model identity, since a hosted model behind a fixed alias
can change [@ChenEtAl2024ChatGPTBehavior]. The response hash pins the retained
output rather than the hosted generator.

Third, the retained prompt copy does not match its recorded identity. Both the
preregistration and runtime provenance name SHA-256
`ec12df200a134532...76fbca`,
while the surviving `model_prompt.md` hashes to
`36e0167aa338c6b...6971`.
No matching prompt copy was found. The complete model response is retained,
but the package cannot verify the exact prompt that produced it. This mismatch
does not change the frozen simulator results or their replay, but it prevents
exact reconstruction of the generation context.

The protocol neither declared nor logged exploratory prompt iterations and
author hours before the freeze. A complete accounting would include that human
cost. The missing field is a limitation discovered after the run, not a frozen
requirement that the study satisfied.

### Interpreting Proposal Overlap

The model proposed 16 by 64, 8 by 128, and 32 by 16. The fixed aspect-ratio
heuristic ranked legal shapes by processing-element count, then by closeness to
the workload's aggregate N-to-M aspect ratio, with a deterministic tie break.
It proposed 16 by 64, 8 by 128, and 64 by 16. The two arms therefore selected
two of the same nonbaseline shapes. Including the shared 32 by 32 baseline, the
union contains five unique evaluated shapes from the fifteen legal shapes.

This overlap matters because the shared choices cannot be attributed uniquely
to the model. The arms agree on two of their three proposals and differ in only
one, where the model's 32 by 16 and the heuristic's 64 by 16 each rank worse.
With only fifteen legal shapes and a model compared against a weak fixed
heuristic that selected many of the same shapes, the comparison had little
resolving power[^fn-resolving-power-c08] to separate them. The result is a
numerical tie and a local non-demonstration of AI advantage, not evidence of
parity between the proposers.

[^fn-resolving-power-c08]: **Resolving power**: A design's ability to separate genuinely different candidates. The evaluation here is deterministic, so the immediate limit is discrimination rather than statistical power over evaluation noise. With few distinct legal shapes and substantial overlap between proposal sets, this comparison had little opportunity to show a difference.

## Reporting Selected Candidates

The validated candidate and workload identities became frozen SCALE-Sim input
configurations. The runner executed eight proposal-arm evaluations and four
shared mechanism probes. All twelve records report `status: ok`, and both the
processing-element and cycle checks pass in every record. The execution
provenance reports zero failures. Input and report hashes bind each evaluation
to its retained files. They do not repair the missing rejected-schema artifacts
or the prompt hash mismatch. Repeated shapes in different arms keep separate
evaluation identities, which preserves the declared arm budgets.

Back in the run that did execute, several legal
alternatives ranked worse under the declared score, and no nonbaseline shape
cleared the decision margin across all eight arm evaluations
(@tbl-ai-study-results).

| **Arm** | **Shape and source** | **Cycles** | **Average layer utilization** | **Local score** | **Result within arm** |

| Heuristic | 64 by 16 proposal | 17,757 | 32.294% | 54,985.25 | Ranked worse |

```{python}
#| label: fig-ai-study-result
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Results of the equal-simulator-call study and declared contrast.** The left panel reports every candidate score under equal four-run simulator budgets. The 32 by 32 baseline and 16 by 64 shape tie in both arms; lower is better. The right panel tests the model's directional prediction. The predicted winner reversal after transposing M and N does not occur. Cycles and utilization come from the retained SCALE-Sim 3.0.0 outputs; the retained runner computes scores and margins. #| out-width: "100%"

import json
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

result_path = Path("../labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/reference/study_results.json")
result = json.loads(result_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

arm_runs = [r for r in result["evaluations"] if r["arm"] in {"model", "conventional"}]
probe_runs = [r for r in result["evaluations"] if r["arm"] == "mechanism_probe"]

shape_labels = {
    "model_baseline_32x32": "M  32×32 baseline",
    "ai_wide_16x64": "M  16×64",
    "ai_extreme_8x128": "M  8×128",

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5.6, 2.65), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.35, 1]})
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.22, right=0.985, top=0.82, bottom=0.18, wspace=0.42)

x = [0, 1]
for shape, color, marker in [("16×64", COLORS["blue"], "o"), ("64×16", COLORS["orange"], "s")]:
```

In the left panel, the 32 by 32 baseline and 16 by 64 candidate have the same
shortest bar in both arms. No nonbaseline shape moves below the baseline. In the
right panel, 16 by 64 remains below 64 by 16 after M and N are exchanged. The
gap narrows, but the lines do not cross.

The first panel shows why no change is
warranted for the five evaluated shapes and why the two proposal arms tie on
the local score derived by the retained runner from simulator outputs. It does
not establish that 32 by 32 is optimal across all fifteen legal shapes or that
the two methods consumed equal total effort. The right panel probes the
mechanism behind these proposals, which requires a dedicated contrast test.

## Testing Matched Contrasts

As shown in the right panel of @fig-ai-study-result, the model predicted that 16 by 64 would beat its mirrored 64 by 16 shape on the
original workload because the wider array would align better with the supplied
N dimensions. It also predicted that exchanging M and N would reverse the
winner. This is a testable prediction because it names a direction and a
failure condition.

Each margin below compares the two shapes on one workload, so the four runs form two within-workload pairs rather than a single cross-workload comparison. On the original workload, 16 by 64 wins by 38.56 percent, with scores of
33,782.40 and 54,985.25. After transposition, it still wins by 7.57 percent,
23,530.65 to 25,458.11. The predicted reversal does not occur. The margin does narrow sharply, evidence that the transposition changed something the failed explanation cannot account for, even though the shift stopped short of a reversal.

The directional prediction therefore fails its declared contrast. The
surviving prompt copy did not pin the mapping semantics, and the package cannot
establish whether the recorded call did. Independently, the contrast did not
isolate orientation. The result therefore neither shows that orientation is
irrelevant nor supplies a replacement explanation.

The mapping-semantic gap in the surviving prompt copy became clear only after
the run. Under SCALE-Sim's weight-stationary GEMM mode, the resident weight
tile is K by N. Array height carries K, array width carries N, and M streams
through the array (@fig-array-mapping). The model's assumption that width
tracks N was conventional, but the retained package cannot establish what
binding the recorded call received or whether the model reasoned from it.

![**The axis binding omitted from the surviving prompt copy.** Under SCALE-Sim's weight-stationary GEMM mode, array height carries K and array width carries N, while M streams through the array. Exchanging M and N leaves K unchanged, so the mirrored shapes move more than one fold count. The contrast tests the recorded directional prediction but does not isolate orientation as a cause.](images/F8-array-mapping){#fig-array-mapping fig-alt="A GEMM workload feeds a resident weight tile of K by N, which maps onto wide 16 by 64 and tall 64 by 16 arrays. K maps over array height and N over array width. A dashed transpose connector notes that K is unchanged, so the mirrored pair changes more than one fold count."}

The transposition still tests the model's exact directional prediction, but it
is not a causally isolated test of orientation. Exchanging M and N leaves K
untouched, while mirroring 16 by 64 and 64 by 16 changes both the N-fold count
on the width axis and the K-fold count on the height axis. The test therefore
probes the prompt's completeness and the contrast design as well as the
model's architectural reasoning. A stronger follow-up must pin the mapping
semantics in the prompt and vary one fold count at a time.

## Judging Claims

With the candidate evaluations and the mechanism contrast complete, the
architect can now resolve the four distinct judgments fixed in the predeclared
study plan. The four conclusions in @tbl-study-claim-dispositions answer
distinctly different questions.

| **Claim** | **Observed evidence** | **Conclusion** | **Outside this conclusion** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Architecture outcome** | Best evaluated nonbaseline ties the baseline; improvement is 0.0%. | No change under the 1 percent decision margin for the five evaluated shapes. | No claim about the ten unevaluated legal shapes, another workload, or another objective. |
| **AI contribution** | Best scores tie at four simulator calls per arm; two nonbaseline selections overlap. | No study-local AI advantage is demonstrated against the weak fixed heuristic. | Total effort is unknown, and no broader claim about a model family follows. |
| **Mechanism explanation** | 16 by 64 wins on both workloads. | The directional prediction fails its declared contrast. | No causally isolated replacement explanation, especially without pinned mapping semantics. |
| **Stopping decision** | No selected candidate clears the decision margin, and post-result replacement is prohibited. | Stop the bounded search and recommend retaining 32 by 32 for the evaluated set. | The architecture action remains pending; 32 by 32 is not claimed optimal among all fifteen legal shapes. |

: **The four judgments have different conclusions.** The architecture outcome, AI contribution, mechanism explanation, and stopping decision remain separate. {#tbl-study-claim-dispositions tbl-colwidths="[19,31,18,32]"}

The first row asks whether any new shape warrants a change under the local
score. The second asks whether the model found an advantage over the heuristic
under the same simulator-call budget. The third tests only the model's
explanation. The fourth records what the architect does next. Each conclusion
follows from different evidence.

A different run could split them. A candidate that cleared the margin would set the architecture outcome to a change and still leave the stopping decision at stop, if the evaluation budget were spent or the gain did not justify the cost of verifying it. In this run no candidate cleared the margin, so the outcome and the stopping decision point the same way, and the mechanism verdict stands apart from both.

The frozen protocol permits no post-result replacement, and no candidate
clears the decision margin, so the technical study stops here. Its
recommendation is to retain 32 by 32 for the five evaluated shapes because a
nonbaseline tie does not justify change under the declared rule. The
architecture action remains pending. A broader workload, another dataflow,
pinned mapping semantics, a calibrated memory model, or implementation-adjacent
constraints would require a new study rather than an extension of this run.

## Closing the Local Record

One completed record keeps the frozen study, its four judgments, and the
pending architecture action together for the next chapter
(@tbl-practitioner-path).

| **Record field** | **Completed local record** |
| --- | --- |
| **Frozen plan** | Three-layer GEMM slice, 32 by 32 baseline, fifteen legal shapes, fixed simulator configuration, local score, 1 percent margin, four calls per proposal arm, and four shared mechanism probes. |
| **Execution** | One pre-inference schema rejection, one schema-valid model response, eight proposal-arm evaluations, four mechanism probes, and five unique evaluated shapes. The retained record supplies call counts and a 19.05-second aggregate runner window, but not per-attempt queue time, run time, compute, memory, storage, or license use. Total human effort remains unknown. |
| **Measurements** | SCALE-Sim cycles, utilization, and modeled memory traffic under the retained inputs and version. No silicon, timing-closure, physical-design, or measured-energy result. |
| **Architecture outcome** | No evaluated nonbaseline shape clears the declared margin. This is a no-change study outcome for the five evaluated shapes, not an optimality result. |
| **Study-local AI contribution** | The model arm and weak fixed heuristic tie on the frozen score under equal simulator-call budgets. The comparison demonstrates no local AI advantage and does not measure total effort or model reliability. |
| **Mechanism status** | The predicted winner reversal does not occur. The directional explanation fails. A replacement mechanism remains unresolved because the surviving prompt copy omitted mapping semantics, the exact recorded context cannot be verified, and the contrast did not isolate orientation. |
| **Stopping and decision status** | The bounded technical study stops. Retaining 32 by 32 is the recorded recommendation, the architecture action remains `awaiting_author_confirmation`, and the record does not name the accountable owner. |
| **Record limits** | The exact model prompt cannot be verified because the retained copy does not match the recorded hash. The rejection checks did not fire inside the study, the score omitted modeled memory traffic, and replay shares the study's simulator, workload, score, and assumptions. |
| **Reopening conditions** | Reopen through a newly frozen study if the workload, objective, dataflow, mapping semantics, simulator, model identity, energy model, implementation constraints, or decision scope changes, or if an independent check contradicts the recorded result. |

: **The completed local record separates outcome from action.** The study is
technically closed, its recommendation is explicit, and the architecture action
remains pending.
{#tbl-practitioner-path tbl-colwidths="[24,66]"}

Read down from the frozen plan through execution and measurements before
reaching the architecture-outcome, AI-contribution, mechanism, and stopping
fields. The final rows state the record limits and the conditions that require
a new study. This order keeps the conclusions attached to what actually ran
and what the tools returned. It also preserves the difference between a
technically closed study and an architecture action that still lacks
confirmation and a named owner. Assigning that owner later would create a
dated post-study action record; it would not rewrite the preregistered roles or
the historical run.

## Auditing the Study After Closure

The frozen outcome and four judgments are already closed. The observations in
this section were made by examining the completed record and therefore audit
the study design rather than extend its chronology. They can motivate a new
study, but they cannot add a metric, replace the comparator, or rescore this
run.

Every proposed candidate passed the processing-element and cycle-limit checks,
so this run demonstrates its three declared control checks only in the passing
direction. It does not exercise the invalid-candidate repair path, the
illegal-shape rejection, or the 90,000-cycle cutoff. A future confirmatory run
can include a positive control, such as a shape that violates the
processing-element budget or a run known to cross the cycle cutoff, and require
the harness to reject it before the proposal arms are scored. Such a control
tests the rejection path without converting the invalid candidate into part of
either arm.

The 16 by 64 candidate exactly matches the baseline's cycles, average layer
utilization, and local score. The exact tie is not a consequence of equal
resources alone, since the 8 by 128 shape also has 1,024 processing elements
yet takes 39 percent more cycles. The layers fold onto 32 by 32 and 16 by 64
in the same number of tiles with no edge waste. In SCALE-Sim's closed form for
this mode, $M + 2h + w - 2$, the shape-dependent pipeline term $2h + w - 2$ is
94 for both. Equal tile counts alone do not produce the tie. The heuristic's
64 by 16 shape folds into the same eighty tiles at full mapping efficiency and
still takes 27.6 percent more cycles.

That arithmetic exposes a weakness in the study design. Under this frozen
dataflow, a paper analysis of fold counts, edge waste, and pipeline cost could
have ranked the cycle behavior of the fifteen legal shapes before simulation.
The simulator calls still provide the evidence used by the frozen protocol,
but a preliminary analytical pass could have avoided spending evaluations on
differences already predicted in closed form. The ten unexecuted shapes remain
outside the reported outcome because the protocol required simulator results,
not paper predictions.

The tie also hides a difference that the frozen score does not use.[^fn-dram-traffic]
The 16 by 64 shape has the same cycles and utilization as the baseline but
twice its modeled DRAM-word writes. On the two simulator-reported axes of
cycles and modeled word writes, the baseline dominates that shared candidate
(@fig-proxy-mismatch). The observation does not change the frozen score or
outcome. It reveals that the score omitted a decision-relevant axis. The
blindness runs both ways. The heuristic's 64 by 16 shape has half the
baseline's modeled word writes and 31 percent fewer total modeled DRAM-word
accesses,
while taking 27.6 percent more cycles. A later energy-aware study could value
that tradeoff differently [@Horowitz2014Energy].

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The omitted memory axis in the 3\ W XR system"}
The modeled write ratio raises a system question rather than answering one.
In the Lighthouse interpretation, an accelerator serving spatial tracking
would share its memory path with the RISC-V host cores and XR display engine,
so extra traffic could consume bandwidth and energy needed elsewhere. The
synthetic workload does not establish that such traffic occurs in the
Lighthouse system, and this study measures neither contention nor physical energy.
SCALE-Sim reports one-byte interface words in this configuration, not
identified DRAM transactions, so converting the counts into energy requires a
memory-system model that this run does not have.
:::

An architect who discovered this proxy mismatch after a run
(@sec-feedback-verification-trust) would not rescore the completed results
against a new objective. A new preregistration could replace the
cycles-and-utilization score with one that prices data movement, such as an
energy-delay product $\text{EDP} = E_{\text{total}} \times \text{cycles}$,
where an architecture-level energy model estimates compute, SRAM, and DRAM
energy [@WuEtAl2019Accelergy]. That would be a new confirmatory study rather
than a rescoring of this one. No such amendment was filed here. This study
reports the tie under the score it froze, and the memory axis remains a stated
limitation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-proxy-mismatch
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **The frozen score omits modeled memory traffic.** The local score ranks the shared 16 by 64 candidate exactly equal to the 32 by 32 baseline. Across two SCALE-Sim outputs, cycles and modeled DRAM-word writes, the baseline dominates that candidate. This post-run observation does not change the frozen outcome; it motivates a new score and study.
#| out-width: "80%"
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of evaluated systolic array shapes using two SCALE-Sim outputs. The 32 by 32 baseline and shared 16 by 64 candidate both take 13,917 cycles, while the shared candidate reports about twice the modeled DRAM-word writes."

import json
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

result_path = Path("../labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/reference/study_results.json")
result = json.loads(result_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

# We will just plot all evaluated runs
arm_runs = [r for r in result["evaluations"] if r["arm"] in {"model", "conventional"}]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 3.5))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.18, right=0.95, top=0.88, bottom=0.15)

ax.set_title("Frozen Score Omits Modeled Memory Traffic", fontsize=7.5, pad=8)
ax.set_xlabel("Compute Cycles (lower is better)", fontsize=6.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Modeled DRAM-word writes (lower is better)", fontsize=6.5)

# Deduplicate points by candidate_id
seen = set()
for r in arm_runs:
    cid = r["candidate_id"]
    if cid in seen: continue
    seen.add(cid)

    cycles = r["gates"]["deadline"]["observed"]
    dram_writes = r["metrics"]["dram_writes"]

    label = cid.replace("model_baseline_", "").replace("ai_wide_", "").replace("ai_extreme_", "").replace("ai_compact_", "").replace("conventional_baseline_", "").replace("heuristic_", "")

    if "32x32" in label:
        color = COLORS["blue"]
        marker = "o"
        label_text = f"Baseline\n{label}"
        ax.plot(cycles, dram_writes, marker=marker, markersize=5, color=color)
        ax.text(cycles - 500, dram_writes - 10000, label_text, color=COLORS["ink"], fontsize=5.5, ha="right", va="top")
    elif "16x64" in label:
        color = COLORS["red"]
        marker = "X"
        label_text = f"Shared candidate\n{label}"
        ax.plot(cycles, dram_writes, marker=marker, markersize=5, color=color)
        ax.text(cycles + 300, dram_writes + 15000, label_text, color=COLORS["ink"], fontsize=5.5, ha="left", va="bottom")
    else:
        color = COLORS["orange"]
        marker = "s"
        ax.plot(cycles, dram_writes, marker=marker, markersize=4, color=color, alpha=0.6)
        ax.text(cycles + 300, dram_writes, label, color=COLORS["ink"], fontsize=5, ha="left", va="center", alpha=0.7)

# Mark the shared minimum-cycle coordinate
ax.axvline(x=13917, color=COLORS["grid"], linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8, zorder=0)

ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=5.9, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(True, color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.55, zorder=0)
for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
```

[^fn-dram-traffic]: At identical cycles and utilization, SCALE-Sim reports 409,726 one-byte DRAM-word writes for 16 by 64 against 204,863 for the baseline, twice as many, and about 1.6 times the total modeled word accesses.

Read toward the lower-left because both axes are lower-is-better simulator
outputs. The baseline and shared 16 by 64 candidate align at 13,917 cycles, but
the shared candidate sits much higher on modeled DRAM-word writes. The baseline
therefore dominates that candidate on these two reported quantities even
though the frozen composite score ties them. The plot exposes an omitted axis;
it does not authorize post-run rescoring or establish physical memory energy.

The 32 by 16 shape has higher average layer utilization than the baseline but
takes far more cycles, so the composite rule ranks it worse. The 8 by 128 shape
loses on both ingredients. A reader who disagrees with the composite score can
still inspect those raw quantities and challenge the rule without rerunning
the study.

An elongated 8 by 128 or 16 by 64 block might also cost more in wire length,
Network-on-Chip (NoC) routing congestion, timing closure, and global
interconnect power than a compact 32 by 32 block. That is a reasonable
hypothesis, but it is not a result of this run. SCALE-Sim performs no timing
closure or physical design, and this run enabled no energy model. Testing the
hypothesis would require a new tier of tooling, such as a floorplan or
place-and-route estimate.

Before a confirmatory run, the evaluator should test whether the proposed
comparison can distinguish the arms. A pilot or analytical pass can estimate
proposal overlap and score sensitivity. The actual comparison should then run
on workloads or cases that were not used to tune the proposal rules, prompt,
heuristic, or score. Evaluator-owned positive controls should exercise the
legality and cutoff paths without entering either proposal arm. The exact
prompt, schema, tool configuration, and preregistration should be bound to the
record before inference. Prompt development, comparator tuning, and score
selection belong to the development phase; confirmation begins only after
those choices are frozen. These changes define a new study. They do not
retroactively strengthen this one.

## Packaging the Study {#sec-ai-study-archive}

The retained package contains the preregistration, complete model response,
recorded provenance, exact simulator inputs, raw summary reports, parsed
results, hashes, tests, and replay code. The prompt-hash mismatch prevents it
from carrying the exact generation context, but the simulator record remains
intact. The study contains no proprietary PDK data or RTL, so no protected
design data required redaction. A production package would also need to protect
confidential inputs. The files are versioned with the repository, although the
package manifest does not itself record a commit identity. The historical
execution record still contains a local executable path, so the package is not
fully path-scrubbed or self-contained.

The [companion README](https://github.com/harvard-edge/arch2/blob/main/labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study/README.md)
lists the retained files, replay commands, and known provenance limits.

### Mapping Artifacts to Review Questions

Each retained artifact answers a specific review question
(@tbl-study-archive).

| **Artifact** | **What it lets a reviewer check** |
| --- | --- |
| **Preregistration** | The recorded chronology declaring claims, candidates per arm, rejection criteria, score, decision margin, repair limit, contrast, and decision boundary before inference and simulation. Without an external timestamp or commit binding, the file does not independently prove precedence. |
| **Model prompt, schema, and full response** | Whether the printed proposals and prediction match the retained response. The prompt copy shows the intended context but cannot establish the exact context because its hash does not match the frozen record. |
| **Provenance record** | Requested model alias, interface, timestamps, exposed settings, usage, response hash, pre-inference error, and unavailable identity fields. |
| **Fixed aspect-ratio heuristic** | Whether its ordering was deterministic and fixed before model or simulator output. |
| **Reference evaluations and execution provenance** | Exact topology, layout, SCALE-Sim configuration, raw run locations, parsed metrics, rejection results, and conclusions for all twelve evaluations. |
| **Reference manifest and replay** | Whether retained files match their hashes and a network-free rerun regenerates every stable input, report, metric, and result. |

: **Each review question maps to a retained artifact.** These files do not establish that the simulator is accurate or the workload representative, and the prompt mismatch leaves one provenance question unresolved. {#tbl-study-archive tbl-colwidths="[26,64]"}

Read from the declaration artifacts to the model and provenance files, then to
the fixed heuristic, raw evaluations, manifest, and replay. The first group
lets a reviewer inspect what was intended and what the model returned. The
second connects those declarations to the executed simulator results and
retained hashes. Together they support review and replay of the recorded
computation, but they do not establish simulator fidelity or workload
representativeness.

### What Each Follow-up Checks

The package supports different follow-up actions that answer different
questions (@tbl-verification-levels). They do not form an automatic hierarchy
in which one result proves the next.

| **Follow-up** | **Study status** | **What a successful result would support** | **What it would not establish** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Reference integrity check** | The retained manifest can be checked against the archived files. | The archived files still match their recorded hashes and sizes. | That the computation can be regenerated or that the simulator is faithful. |
| **Deterministic simulator replay** | A network-free replay path is packaged; completion must be reported separately. | The retained runner, simulator version, inputs, and parsing regenerate the stable study outputs. | Simulator fidelity, workload representativeness, or an independent result. |
| **Generator re-execution** | Exact reproduction is unavailable because provider revision and seed were not exposed and the retained prompt hash does not match. | A new call could measure behavior of the currently available model and runtime. | Recreation of the recorded proposal or truth of the architecture claim. |
| **Independent architecture check** | Not performed. | A different implementation or testbench could test whether the local result or proposed mechanism survives different modeling assumptions. | Automatic removal of every shared specification, workload, or modeling error. |

: **Each follow-up has a bounded meaning.** Replay tests computational
repeatability under shared assumptions; a separately designed check can reduce
some shared assumptions without becoming ground truth. {#tbl-verification-levels tbl-colwidths="[20,22,30,28]"}

Read downward as four different questions rather than four levels of proof.
Reference integrity asks whether the retained files changed. Simulator replay
asks whether the same computation can be regenerated. Generator re-execution
tests current behavior without recreating the recorded call, while an
independent architecture check changes part of the modeling path. Success in
one row cannot supply the conclusion reserved for another.

### Verifying the Replay

The preregistration records what was declared before inference. The model
artifacts retain the response while exposing the prompt-identity gap. The raw
reports and parsed results show what SCALE-Sim returned, and the manifest and
replay code connect the reported numbers back to retained files. Together,
those records let another architect check the declared simulator computation
without implying that SCALE-Sim is accurate enough for a different claim or
that the workload represents the full system intent.

Offline replay needs no network account or model credential. It verifies the
reference, reruns all twelve evaluations, and compares their stable inputs,
summary reports, metrics, and hashes. Large deterministic access traces are
regenerated rather than archived. That choice assumes the pinned simulator
version and configuration regenerate the traces used for the reported
metrics. The package compares stable summary reports and parsed results; any
disagreement requires investigation rather than a presumption about which
artifact is correct.

An optional provider-neutral live adapter writes to a separate output directory
and checks the requested model alias. That check does not recover the exact
provider revision or digest used for the recorded call. The adapter halts if the
runtime or credential is unavailable, the response is invalid, or a proposed
geometry is illegal. It never changes the recorded reference results. Commands
and failure details remain in the companion rather than the printed chapter.

A successful replay confirms that the retained computation can be regenerated
under the retained code and inputs in a compatible environment matching the
documented versions. It is not an independent
result because it shares the same runner, simulator, workload, score, and
assumptions. It does not validate SCALE-Sim against fabricated silicon,
establish workload representativeness, justify the local score or thresholds,
resolve the missing mapping semantics, or predict another model call. Those
are new claims requiring new evidence.

## Open Research Questions

The null result is useful because it exposes the questions that this study
could not answer.

### Objectives and Representation

**How should an energy-relevant axis enter a selection score?** A fast
simulator can report a precise ranking while omitting the cost that changes the
decision, but an unvalidated energy term can be just as misleading.

**What would make an architecture-level energy model adequate for candidate
selection?** A post-run sensitivity calculation can identify a missing axis
without establishing that the model is faithful enough to guide search.

**How should mapping semantics be represented before a mechanism is tested?**
A dataflow name alone does not bind workload dimensions to array dimensions,
and an omitted binding can make the contrast test the prompt rather than the
mechanism.

**How can a proposal and its explanation be evaluated separately?** A useful
candidate may arrive with a false explanation, while a failed candidate can
still state a mechanism worth testing elsewhere.

### Study Discrimination and Controls

**How can a study test its resolving power before execution?** A small
candidate space and overlapping proposal rules can make a tie likely even when
the underlying proposers differ.

**Which candidates can be screened analytically before simulation?** A paper
model of fold counts and pipeline cost can reserve expensive tool calls for
questions the simple model cannot settle.

**How should a study exercise rejection checks that no real candidate
triggers?** Positive controls can test the rejecting direction without
changing the proposal-arm budgets or entering the invalid candidate into the
architecture comparison.

### Independent Checking and Transfer Limits

**What independent check best challenges a simulator result?** A different
implementation can reduce shared tool assumptions while still sharing the
same specification, workload, or blind spot.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Close four judgments, not one success story"}
A completed study reports the architecture outcome, study-local AI
contribution, mechanism status, and stopping result separately. A tie, failed
explanation, or pending recommendation must remain visible rather than being
combined into a claim that the study succeeded.
:::

This bounded study ends with a numerical tie against the baseline. The model
and fixed aspect-ratio heuristic selected five unique datapath shapes from
fifteen legal shapes, and no evaluated nonbaseline shape cleared the 1 percent
decision margin over 32 by 32. That is a no-change outcome under the frozen
rule, not a completed architecture action. The technical study stops with a
recommendation to retain 32 by 32. The action remains
`awaiting_author_confirmation`, and the record names no accountable owner. The
tie also reveals the comparison's low resolving power. The two arms shared most
of their selected shapes in a small search space.

The declared contrast tested the model's directional prediction, which failed
to produce the anticipated reversal. The frozen simulator settings, score,
and decision margin make a post-run change visible, but they do not repair the
unpinned mapping semantics or the mismatched prompt record. The failed
explanation remains failed, and the post-run memory finding motivates a new
study rather than a revised score for this one.

Catching the schema error before inference shows why structured output must be
validated before it becomes a simulator action. One study does not validate
the book's complete approach or a model family. It shows how to bind one
proposal to a frozen comparison, report a tie without promoting it, test an
explanation separately, and expose limits in the surviving record. A
successful replay checks the retained simulator computation under shared
assumptions. Exact generator reproduction is unavailable, and no independent
architecture check was performed.

The result handed to @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack is deliberately local.
It includes the frozen plan, recorded execution, simulator measurements, four
judgments, pending recommendation, score and prompt limitations, nonclaims,
and reopening conditions. The next question is not whether this one result
generalizes. It is what must be re-established when the target architecture
decision changes.
